item.title: It’s finally farm bill week
item.content:encoded:
Presented by Bayer: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

Presented by Bayer

With help from Grace Yarrow and Meredith Lee Hill

House Agriculture Chair Glenn Thompson (R-Pa.) at the Capitol. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
QUICK FIX

— The House will vote on the farm bill this week, and the Supreme Court will hear arguments on a contentious pesticide labeling case.

— A USDA union invoked its right to bargain over the closure of day cares located in department buildings.

— A new Capitol area ad buy advocates blocking Proposition 12 through federal legislation.

IT’S MONDAY, APRIL 27. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send tips and pitches to rshin@politico.com and follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

THE MOMENT OF TRUTH: The House will vote on the farm bill Thursday, as Meredith reported over the weekend.

The legislation faces a narrow path forward as some Republicans, including Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.), threaten to oppose it unless its pesticide labeling language is removed. With the GOP’s slim majority, even a small cadre of Republicans could block the bill’s passage as most Democrats also plan to vote against it.

The provision, which would prevent pesticide makers from being sued over cancer warning labeling, is the biggest source of conflict surrounding the bill, as Grace and Meredith reported. However, other potential “yes” voters are also threatening to vote “no” over myriad issues.

President Donald Trump and many Republican lawmakers have said they feel urgency to pass the bill, which could sway rural voters in November’s midterm elections, especially as farm country struggles with the high costs of fertilizer and fuel stemming from the war in Iran.

Other big questions about the legislation’s final form loom ahead of Thursday, and the House Rules Committee will meet at 1 p.m. today to consider hundreds of amendments on issues including pesticides, food aid and the blocking of California’s Proposition 12.

Rep. Andrew Garbarino (R-N.Y.) told MA Sunday that his top request is a vote on an amendment to remove the “Save Our Bacon Act,” which would overturn Proposition 12, from the bill. He said he hasn’t gotten an indication of whether the Rules Committee or leaders will push for a vote on it.

He said he won’t oppose a procedural vote on the rule but that his vote on final passage will depend on how the bill changes during the Rules process.

“I know some of my colleagues are not happy with my stance — one of them told me I was breaking his heart,” Garbarino said, adding that he was concerned about how the bill would affect existing rules and regulations in New York.

“So I think we have to be very careful about the way all this all moves forward,” he said.

A bipartisan amendment introduced by Rep. Michelle Fischbach (R-Minn.) would allow the year-round sale of E15 and reform the Renewable Fuel Standard. The proposal had 20 co-sponsors, including House Rural Domestic Energy Council Co-Chairs Randy Feenstra (R-Iowa) and Stephanie Bice (R-Okla.).

While year-round E15 enjoys widespread bipartisan support among ag-state lawmakers, Ag Committee leaders have said the issue is not in its jurisdiction, so it would require a waiver from House leadership to be lumped into the farm bill. It is unclear whether Speaker Mike Johnson will grant the waiver.

Where the Dems stand: Two of the seven Democrats who voted to advance the farm bill out of committee, Reps. Josh Riley (D-N.Y.) and Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Mich.) told MA that they plan to vote for it again on the floor. But Republicans will likely still have to count on centrist Democrats voting for the bill to have a chance at passage due to infighting over the contentious provisions.

Also on the Hill this week: The House Appropriations Committee will mark up the Ag-FDA budget for fiscal 2027 Tuesday. It is expected to run late into the night and could spill into Wednesday.
 

A message from Bayer:

86% of Americans think science misinformation is getting worse according to new data from a survey conducted by The Harris Poll on behalf of Bayer. When that misinformation targets modern farming practices, the fallout is real. Farmers face regulatory uncertainty while consumers grow more anxious about food safety. Still, a bipartisan majority of Americans agree; rigorous, evidence-based science is necessary for the country’s future. Dig into the numbers.
 
IN THE COURTS

ON THE DOCKET: The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments today for Monsanto v. Durnell, a case that has been at the center of the political battle over glyphosate, the active ingredient in the herbicide Roundup.

The case weighs whether Bayer, which acquired Monsanto in 2018, should be preempted from failure-to-warn claims for cancer risks associated with pesticide use.

It has been a political flash point between the Make America Healthy Again movement and the White House. The Trump administration filed a brief in December in support of the chemical company and released an executive order aiming to boost production of glyphosate earlier this year.

MAHA leaders are hosting a rally titled “The People vs. Poison” at 9 a.m. in front of the high court. Speakers will include MAHA advocates Vani Hari and Tony Lyons and Reps. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) and Thomas Massie (R-Ky.).
 

A message from Bayer:
 
AT THE AGENCIES

FIRST IN MA: The Department of Agriculture and one of its staff unions will begin facing off today over the department’s planned day care closures.

The USDA Child Development Center will cease operations this summer after the company running the facility declined to sign a new contract with the department, as your host first reported last week.

But Collin Bradley, president of AFSCME Local 3976, which represents staff at the Foreign Agricultural Service, said the union did not receive notice of the closures from the USDA itself, as required by its bargaining agreement.

KinderCare notified USDA parents that the day cares in the department’s Yates Building and the George Washington Carver Center would close on July 10, according to two KinderCare emails obtained by POLITICO.

“I think one of the things that has angered people so much is the complete lack of communication or care from the department level,” Bradley told MA. “It seems like they're not even telling their subagencies about it and they're just leaving employees in a lurch.”

Bradley said USDA has also not fulfilled a union contract child care provision related to the department’s sweeping reorganization plans.

“We have a specific language about if they move employees away from the South building, they have to do a survey of the employees, see what the child care needs are and then make changes based on those recommendations,” Bradley said. “That has not been done yet, even though it's been a year since they announced that they're moving people out.”

USDA announced in July 2025 that it would relocate much of its Washington-area staff to regional hubs across the country. Deputy Agriculture Secretary Stephen Vaden has said he expects employees will move to their reassigned locations this summer, coinciding with the day cares’ closure.

USDA spokesperson Alec Varsamis said in a statement that “the impending closure of the KinderCare facility in the Yates Building has nothing to do with the Department’s reorganization; as has been made clear, the Yates building will remain and continue to house USDA employees.”

Some USDA employees who use the day cares said the closures will mean added strain to their lives, longer commutes and possibly higher costs, as department employees pay a subsidized lower fee to enroll in the in-house child care.

Union representatives are scheduled to meet with USDA’s labor relations staff Monday afternoon to begin a bargaining process over the planned closure. Bradley said that because child care is an essential service, it is incumbent upon USDA to find another day care vendor for the space.
 

A message from Bayer:

Misinformation about agricultural science spreads faster than facts, creating uncertainty for farmers and policymakers alike. Yet here's what the data show: 88% of Republicans and 92% of Democrats agree rigorous science is necessary for progress. Americans haven't given up on evidence-based science - they're exhausted by viral misinformation and hungry for credibility.

A new survey conducted by The Harris Poll on behalf of Bayer on what Americans actually think about science and trust. The results reveal both challenge and opportunity - and shows policymakers that Americans value continued investment in research, innovation, and the scientific process.

See the findings for yourself and voice your support for science and the evidence-based outcomes it brings. Learn more.
 
Influence and Industry

MA EXCLUSIVE: The Center for the Environment and Welfare is rolling out an ad buy in the Washington, D.C., market this week in opposition to California’s Proposition 12, coinciding with the anticipated vote on the farm bill.

The commercial argues Proposition 12 has elevated grocery prices. It will air on CNN, MSNBC’s “Morning Joe,” and Fox News’ “Fox & Friends.”

“Farmers have to spend millions and millions of dollars to rebuild barns to be California compliant,” the ad says. “Those costs are passed on to consumers across America, even if they don't live in California, and low-income Americans are being hit hardest.”

“Congress is considering a fix that will help reduce your food costs and mix California's law before it gets worse,” it continues.

Dozens of House Democrats recently sent a letter to the chamber’s leadership opposing the provision, and it’s unclear whether it will remain in the final text amid opposition from some Republicans including Garbarino.
Row Crops

— Canada is launching a new forestry strategy as the sector continues to get walloped by the Trump administration’s trade war, our Zi-Ann Lum reports.

— First lady Melania Trump announced in a post on X the addition of a beehive housing two colonies to the White House honey program.

item.content:encoded:
Presented by Growth Energy: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

Presented by Growth Energy

With help from Grace Yarrow

“I think we need to have a serious conversation about SNAP and, in particular, the way we calculate it,” said Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.). | Francis Chung/POLITICO
QUICK FIX

— Senate Ag Democrats want changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program’s cost-sharing model included in the chamber's farm bill.

— More than a dozen projects at the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center are set to be eliminated or have their funding reduced due to budget cuts, according to an audio recording of an all-hands meeting.

— Food aid groups expressed concern that reorganization of the Department of Agriculture’s nutrition program employees will interfere with the distribution of assistance.

IT’S MONDAY, MAY 4. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send tips to rshin@politico.com. Follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

TODAY: Jonathan Greenberger kicks off his first week as Global Editor-in-Chief for POLITICO. In a note shared with readers and subscribers, Greenberger spoke to how innovation has been part of POLITICO’s DNA from the start and emphasized continuing to evolve the ways we deliver our journalism. Read the full note here.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
 

A message from Growth Energy:

American farmers are speaking out: Year-round E15 is a win for everyone. It delivers lower-cost fuel for drivers, stronger markets for farmers, and greater U.S. energy security. Congress must act NOW to unlock affordable options at the pump.
 
DRIVING THE DAY

RENEWED DEMANDS: Several Senate Democrats said their support for the House’s version of the farm bill is contingent on changes to the cost-share framework for SNAP that were enacted last summer as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

“We need to have a bicameral negotiation between the House and the Senate on a bipartisan farm bill,” Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.) told MA. “That negotiation has to include some sort of relief on the drastic cuts to SNAP. I hear about this as much from Republican county commissioners in Minnesota as from anyone because they're very worried about the big cost shifts that are involved.”

Senate Ag ranking member Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) said in a statement after the House passed its farm bill Thursday that committee Democrats are “committed to ensuring all states are treated equally by delaying the new SNAP cost shifts.”

The Republican megalaw requires states with SNAP error rates of 6 percent and above to split the financial burden of the program with the federal government. Some state officials have said the plan could leave them unable to afford to run the program at full capacity.

“I think we need to have a serious conversation about SNAP and, in particular, the way we calculate it,” said Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.). “I'm glad it's over here in the Senate and we can actually now get to it, even if we still have some big differences between us.”

Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) said the House legislation “did nothing to help states that are going to be devastated” by SNAP cuts.

The Senate faces a tight timeline for negotiating, passing and delivering a farm bill to President Donald Trump’s desk before Congress’ August recess. The path is further complicated by an array of other bills competing for the chamber’s attention ahead of midterm elections.

“We've got a couple of banking measures that could consume a lot of time, so you could just run out of runway, and we've got to prioritize,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said. “If I've got a choice between some of those issues and getting the NDAA and farm bill out, then I've got to favor NDAA and farm bill.”

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) said the year-round E15 bill that was decoupled from the farm bill is a higher priority for him than the farm bill.

“Year-round E15 is so much more important than what’s left of the farm bill. We passed the important things on the farm bill already,” Marshall told MA Thursday. “That’s my focus right now.”
 

A message from Growth Energy:
 
AROUND THE AGENCIES

FIRST IN MA: More than a dozen research projects underway at the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center will be terminated or receive reduced funding, Agricultural Research Service Administrator Joon Park said at an all-hands meeting, according to an audio recording obtained by MA.

The internal meeting came after USDA announced it would move most of its research and economics employees to regional hubs and start the process of decommissioning the research complex in Maryland.

BARC employees received emails last week about whether their research will continue to be funded and whether they will be relocated from the Washington area, according to two sources familiar and two versions of the notice previously obtained by MA.

Park said a “group of our colleagues at BARC received a notification stating that the FY26 congressional funding budget from Congress for this fiscal year terminated nine research projects at BARC, as well as reduced funding for eight research projects at BARC,” per the recording.

Employees working on those projects will receive a letter reassigning them to vacancies at ARS, Park added.

A USDA spokesperson told MA in a statement that for fiscal 2026, Congress reduced ARS funding for research in certain areas by over $32 million and increased spending for "higher priority" projects.

"For BARC, this resulted in the elimination of funding for 9 research projects and reduction of funding for 8 research projects across the areas of crop protection, livestock protection, and food safety," the spokesperson said in a statement. "The remaining funding and associated research for those 8 projects with reduced funding will be reassigned to other ARS locations."

More context: The House Appropriations Committee advanced a fiscal 2027 Agriculture-FDA funding bill last month that included a provision that would block USDA from using funds to close ARS facilities without prior notification to Congress.
 

A message from Growth Energy:

Across the country, farmers are calling on Congress to pass year-round E15. Made with homegrown energy, E15 lowers costs for American families, supports rural economies, and strengthens our nation’s energy security. Congress can act NOW to give consumers more choices at the pump while supporting U.S. agriculture. Discover why farmers across the country support year-round E15.
 
Food Security Outlook

REORG BACKLASH: Food aid groups slammed the Trump administration’s decision to move USDA’s Food and Nutrition Service employees across the country as part of the department’s sweeping reorganization plan, saying the move could worsen the operation of federal nutrition programs.

“These changes could undermine the close working relationships between State WIC Agencies and regional offices that are essential to day-to-day program operations,” Georgia Machell, president and CEO of the National WIC Association, said in a statement.

“It also offers no plan to retain experienced FNS staff or prevent the loss of institutional knowledge as employees are asked to relocate to new offices across the country,” Machell added.

FNS administers SNAP, the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children and free and reduced-cost school meals.

Thirty percent of FNS staff has already departed in the last year, in part due to offers of deferred resignation.

“I do not share their confidence that this reorg ‘will not disrupt program execution,’ especially since FNS is already so short-staffed,” Katie Bergh, senior policy analyst for food assistance at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, said on X.
Row Crops

— Trump approved state permits for the 2026 red snapper recreational fishing season for Florida, Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina.

— The food industry sees a threat in Kennedy’s push to define “ultraprocessed” food. (The New York Times)

— Junk food is cheaper than healthful food, but a new study reinforces that taste preferences play a bigger role than prices. (The Washington Post Opinion)

item.title: E15 dreams
item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Grace Yarrow and Rachel Shin

An ethanol plant is pictured. | Scott Olson/Getty Images
QUICK FIX

— The clock is ticking for Congress to deliver on permanent year-round E15 promises.

— The United Nations’ international food price index rose for the third consecutive month.

— The Department of Agriculture issued a final rule to implement a law reinstating whole milk in school meals.

IT’S MONDAY, MAY 11. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! We're your hosts, Grace Yarrow and Rachel Shin. Send tips, pitches and exclusives to gyarrow@politico.com and rshin@politico.com. Follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

E15’S ‘BEST BET IN A WHILE’: The House is back in town this week with a familiar but politically potent demand hanging over it: deliver permanent, year-round access to E15.

Vulnerable Midwestern Republicans, farm industry groups and even President Donald Trump have endorsed and pushed for the plan as a boon for corn growers and consumers ahead of the midterm elections. But fierce opposition from oil state lawmakers who argue it will hurt refiners could lead to another fight that might tank the plan.

House leaders infuriated farm state Republicans last month when they agreed to remove the ethanol bill from consideration alongside the farm bill at the last minute amid outcry from oil state Republicans. It was the second time this year that an E15 deal had been punted.

This week, lawmakers are set to vote on a procedural motion that would formally decouple E15 from the farm bill. Then they would vote on the final passage of the E15 plan.

The expected vote could put Speaker Mike Johnson in the position of having to alienate part of his caucus and risk his standing in the House — especially after Trump put him on the hook for delivering on E15.

Vice President JD Vance was in Des Moines last week alongside Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, campaigning for Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa) and touting Republicans’ work on E15.

“We’ve got a lot of Iowa farmers that would love to sell more E15 into the market, and we’re fighting every day to help them,” Vance said, noting that Nunn has been working on legislation on the matter. “We’re working on it every single day.”

Biofuels backers are warning it could be a make-or-break issue for Republicans in November, pointing to nearly 10 swing districts in the Midwest that could shift the balance of power in the House.

“Does [Johnson] really want to hold on to the gavel?” asked one biofuels lobbyist. “Because at this rate, he won't — not when he's rolling 20 Midwesterners who have been crystal clear that we need this.”

“Candidly, since we [postponed] it months ago, there was real danger that that was going to be indefinitely delayed,” Nunn told POLITICO last month. “You know where I stand on E15. I’m going to make sure it comes to the floor in the same way we just did the farm bill.”

As you’ll recall: Trump said during a trip to Clive, Iowa, in January that Congress was “very close” to getting a deal on E15, acknowledging its importance in the region.

“I will sign it without delay, OK? I hope you remember us for the midterms,” Trump said at the time.

Reality check: Even if GOP leaders are able to overcome the House’s divide on the issue, the proposal would face an uncertain future in the Senate.

“God only knows” what will happen if the E15 bill is sent to the Senate, said one agriculture lobbyist who was granted anonymity to discuss the negotiations candidly.

“We've expended a lot of resources and time and effort to get this done in the House,” the lobbyist added. “It's our best bet in a while. We'll deal with that problem [in the Senate] when it arrives.”

One Republican Senate staffer who works for an opponent of the plan said the House’s proposal is a “nonstarter.”

“It won’t pass in the Senate. I feel very confident about that,” the staffer said.
Cost of Living

EYEWATERING PRICES: International food prices climbed for the third consecutive month in April, hitting their highest mark in over three years, according to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization.

The FAO’s food price index rose 1.6 percent from its March level. Much of the increase was driven by a 5.9 percent hike in the vegetable oil index, which reached its highest level since July 2022.

The increase lines up with the war in Iran’s disruption of the fertilizer and energy supply chains.

“The input costs are starting to be transmitted to the commodity prices, but at a very low pace,” FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero said. “The major increase is happening on vegetable oils.”

The global meat price index also climbed to a record high, rising 1.2 percent from March and up 6.4 percent from April 2025. The FAO attributed high meat prices to limited slaughter-ready supply and ongoing efforts to rebuild herds.

Torero warned that strengthening safety net programs for both farmers and consumers will be crucial if global food supply chains continue to be strained.

“We need to accelerate and be prepared in terms of social protection programs in case food prices start to rise significantly,” Torero said. “In the medium term, the recommendation is to assure that farmers can survive because their margins are very small.”
AROUND THE AGENCIES

GOT MILK? USDA issued a final rule allowing schools to serve whole and 2 percent milk, implementing the Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act that Trump signed into law in January.

“President Trump promised to Make America Healthy Again, and restoring whole milk to schools is a major step toward delivering on that promise,” Rollins said in a statement Friday.

The final rule gives schools guidance on returning whole and 2 percent milk to schools that participate in the National School Lunch Program, reversing Obama-era restrictions that limited products with high levels of saturated fat.

It is part of a process to align school meal standards with the new Dietary Guidelines for Americans, according to the department’s announcement.
Row Crops

— It’s time for Trump’s B-Team, the agency understudies who may step into leadership voids, to have a moment. Read POLITICO’s analysis of agency deputies who could later enter the spotlight, including USDA’s Stephen Vaden.

—Sens. Steve Daines (R-Mont.), Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), and Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) held meetings in Beijing and discussed opening China’s markets to agriculture trade across beef, wheat, potatoes and other sectors.

— The Trump administration plan to reorganize food aid employees drew ire from federal workers. (The Washington Post)

— Consumers aren’t cutting back on fast food, even as other costs climb. (The New York Times)

item.title: The GOP’s food fight
item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Grace Yarrow

With help from Marcia Brown

American consumers are only just beginning to feel the impact of a convergence of crises that are raising the cost of food at every step. | Erin Hooley/AP Photo
QUICK FIX

— The Iran war is forcing Republicans to confront the distressing reality that food prices likely won't drop before the midterm elections.

— The White House is weighing how to move forward with executive actions designed to bring down the cost of beef.

— President Donald Trump’s trip to Beijing produced new markets for U.S. meat and other ag products — though details are scarce.

IT'S MONDAY, MAY 18. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Grace Yarrow, filling in while my colleagues are out this week. Send tips, farm bill hot takes and other thoughts to gyarrow@politico.com. And, as always, follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

(GROCERY) BILLS, BILLS, BILLS: American consumers are only just beginning to feel the impact of a convergence of crises — prompted by war, weather and trade policy — that are raising the cost of food at every step, from fields to grocery shelves.

Consumer prices in April rose at their highest rate since May 2023, according to most recent inflation data, thanks largely to ballooning energy costs prompted by the shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz. A separate indicator that often previews inflation that will later hit consumers had its highest monthly gain in four years in April.

And the vise on consumer prices is tightening at the worst moment for Trump and the GOP as they campaign on economic stewardship ahead of November’s elections.

“If we're not really concerned about the midterms, then Republicans must be living in a cave,” Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) said of the impact of rising food prices.

How we got here: Fertilizer prices have skyrocketed, forcing farmers to reconsider how many acres they plant. Diesel fuel prices, which have shot to near-record levels since the war began, have made it more expensive to truck and refrigerate food. Even the cost of oil-based packaging like plastic has started to tick up.

Farmers are bracing for a super El Niño weather pattern that is expected to hammer crops with extreme rains and drought this year. And parched land in the West has already pushed ranchers to sell off much of their cattle, leading to record-high beef prices.

The Trump administration's tariffs have increased the price of critical supplies like aluminum — which is also affected by the closing of the strait — as well as some fresh produce, costs that parts of the food industry are already passing on to consumers, economists say.

"You have a perfect storm in this right now hitting food," said Jason Miller, a professor of supply chain management at Michigan State University.

Voters are already feeling the pain: Seventy-three percent of Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 say food prices have increased greatly or somewhat since the president took office, according to a new POLITICO Poll conducted by Public First from May 9-11. More than half of Americans ranked the cost of living as a top issue facing the United States.

Don’t miss the full story from Marcia here.

SPEAKING OF FOOD PRICES: The White House is deciding how to proceed with a potential executive order that officials hope will address a politically fraught domestic policy challenge that has vexed top aides for months: sky-high beef prices.

Trump planned last week to sign an executive order to ease tariffs on imported beef temporarily — a move that was delayed amid intense backlash from farm-state lawmakers and industry allies.

The executive order could help lower prices for consumers, though by how much remains uncertain. But doing so would drive up competition for American ranchers as they simultaneously face a host of higher costs brought on, in part, by the Iran war.

It’s not the first time Trump has been caught between pleasing ranchers, a loyal GOP constituency, and addressing affordability. But calls for consumer relief are growing as beef prices in the U.S. soar, rising another 2.7 percent, on average, just last month.

Ground beef — a staple of summer cookouts — is approaching $7 a pound, up roughly 12 percent from last summer.

“[Trump] owns hotels and country clubs. They buy beef. He’s acutely aware of it,” said a person close to the White House, who added that while there’s still hope the president can lower prices, there are fears relief won’t reach voters in time.

“You worry that people aren’t feeling it by the time Election Day rolls around,” said the person, granted anonymity to discuss the matter candidly.

Still, Republicans on the Hill are warning the administration that reducing tariffs on imported beef could hardly come at a worse time. Ranchers are already struggling with drought and the threat of the parasitic New World screwworm that could further shrink the country’s small herd — one of the root causes of high prices.

“I know that there were efforts, lobbying efforts, made to explain to the White House the challenges that creates for agriculture producers, presumably ranchers,” Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) said.

Don’t miss the full story from Myah Ward, your host and Daniel Desrochers.
EYE ON CHINA

MORE DETAILS? The White House announced China will purchase at least $17 billion of U.S. ag products per year for the next three years following Trump’s trip to Beijing last week.

Agriculture industry groups and Republican allies were anticipating the president could make progress on new trade agreements or solidify those negotiated last year.

The White House also touted that China restored market access for beef producers by renewing hundreds of expired export licenses, according to a fact sheet published Sunday. China also will resume imports of poultry from U.S. states that the Department of Agriculture has determined have no avian influenza.

Read more from POLITICO’s Ari Hawkins here.
AROUND THE AGENCIES

PERSONNEL MOVES: Aubrey Bettencourt, USDA’s top conservation official, told employees she was stepping down Friday, according to four people familiar with the news and an email obtained by MA.

Associate Chief Colton Buckley will “assume the role of Chief” of the Natural Resources Conservation Service effective today, according to the email Bettencourt sent to staff Friday. Buckley is a Turning Point USA alum and previously was CEO of the National Association of Resource Conservation and Development Councils.

“I could not be more confident in this decision, prouder of what we have accomplished, or more excited of what is to come for our Service,” Bettencourt wrote in the email.

Next up: Bettencourt is moving to a role at the Interior Department, according to two of the people familiar with the talks, who were granted anonymity to discuss the not-yet-public personnel change.

“I'm not going far — I will continue advocating for the farmers and ranchers we serve every day,” Bettencourt wrote.

Read the full scoop from Marcia and yours truly here.
On the Hill

FIRST IN MA: The Independent Beef Association of North Dakota is urging the Trump administration to investigate an “extraordinary” drop in the cattle futures market last October.

When Trump suggested in the fall that he would roughly double the tariff-free quota for Argentine beef, the futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange “collapsed and recovered for contracts that were due long before any increase in imported beef would occur,” the group wrote. They estimated cattle ranchers suffered losses of more than $104 million as a result.

“We ask that your agencies investigate whether market manipulation or other illegal acts caused prices to fall as much as they did,” they wrote.
Transitions

Brad Matsik will be the head of Wells Fargo’s new Food, Beverage and Agribusiness division.
Row Crops

— House Ag Chair G.T. Thompson (R-Pa.) and ranking member Angie Craig (D-Minn.) wrote a letter to Trump urging him to appoint a full panel of bipartisan commissioners to the Commodities Future Trading Commission.

item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Grace Yarrow

With help from Ari Hawkins

Rotisserie chickens may soon be allowed to be purchased using SNAP benefits. | Charlie Riedel/AP Photo
QUICK FIX

— Could rotisserie chicken become an eligible purchase under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program?

— A debate over whether to delay Republicans’ major funding change to SNAP could complicate the Senate’s farm bill hopes.

— Negotiations to reauthorize a trade deal that the ag industry has said is key are set to loom large during meetings between U.S. and Mexican officials this week.

IT’S TUESDAY, MAY 26. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Grace Yarrow, coming back after a very rainy long weekend. Send tips to gyarrow@politico.com or via Signal at gracemy.31. As always, follow your favorite ag team at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
 

POLITICO Pro

Navigate policy challenges with confidence. POLITICO Pro gives professionals authoritative reporting, expert analysis and powerful tools to understand the business of government — in Washington and beyond. Learn more about POLITICO Pro.

 
 
DRIVING THE DAY

WINNER, WINNER, CHICKEN DINNER: Congress is poised to make a major change to the nation’s largest food aid program — by allowing participants to use benefits to buy rotisserie chicken.

In an overwhelming 384-35 vote last month, House lawmakers added legislation to the farm bill that allows rotisserie chicken — but not other hot foods — to be purchased using SNAP benefits amid a broader partisan debate over the program’s future.

The amendment, offered by Rep. Rick Crawford (R-Ark.), faced some bipartisan backlash in the House but appears on track to becoming law as part of the farm bill — in what would be an unprecedented change to SNAP’s design.

In the higher chamber: Senate Ag Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) said he thinks the measure has a “good chance” of being included in the final farm bill.

“It was very popular in the House,” said Boozman. “A lot of our members favor it, so we'll have to wait and see.”

Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.), who co-sponsored the bipartisan Senate bill, said he’s pushing to include the language in the Senate farm bill.

“Why in the world wouldn’t we want to have children and families to be able to have warm meals if we can?” Justice said. “And I just hope to goodness that we can secure it over here on this side.”

Some background: SNAP benefits have excluded all hot foods for decades, with the exception of certain flexibilities following natural disasters or in states that opt to allow households with elderly or disabled people to use SNAP at restaurants.

Katie Bergh, senior policy analyst for food assistance at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, said participants should be allowed to use benefits to purchase foods that “best fit their needs” — given that the average benefit per person is around $6 per day.

“It's pretty limited funds,” Bergh said. “If someone you know is a working parent who is not just limited in funding for groceries but is also extremely limited in time, the ability to purchase a hot item at a grocery store could make a big difference for their family.”

But, but, but: A bipartisan group of lawmakers, anti-hunger groups and industry leaders argue the rotisserie chicken amendment could lead to huge changes for a food aid program that has been designed around groceries, not hot foods.

“We all know that once you add one thing, more things will get added,” said Stephanie Johnson, vice president for government relations at the National Grocers Association.

NGA and retailers have pushed for strong parameters to be implemented alongside allowing any hot foods to be purchased with benefits.

“We, in general, have been opposed to adding hot foods to SNAP just because we know how much more it costs us on the grocery side,” Johnson said.

Even groups that support added flexibility in SNAP are warning against adding just one item to the program without larger reforms around hot foods — leading some Democrats to vote against the farm bill amendment.

“Legislating on an item-by-item basis and cherry-picking what foods are or aren't allowed is not exactly the best model of good governance,” Bergh said. “That's potentially opening up the door to restricting specific items that would leave people with fewer choices and fewer options.

“Once you start legislating on an item-by-item basis, you're potentially adding unnecessary complexity and confusion for participants,” she added.

House Ag Chair G.T. Thompson (R-Pa.), who voted for the amendment, raised concerns about it during farm bill debate on the House floor last month.

“I have concerns about the unintended consequences that may arise should Congress begin to chip away piecemeal at the ban on hot food in SNAP without considering the broader ramifications, particularly for program integrity,” Thompson said.

Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Mich.), who co-sponsored Crawford’s House bill, called the “slippery slope” argument “just an excuse not to do anything."

“Why wouldn’t we make some progress on making life just a little bit easier on people that we know are already financially struggling?” McDonald Rivet told MA. “Anybody who has ever tried to get dinner on the table quickly knows rotisserie chicken is your lifesaver.”
On the Hill

A FARM BILL FACEOFF: Senators are gearing up for a fight over how the farm bill should address Republicans’ historic cuts to SNAP spending when they come back from this week’s recess.

As you’ll recall: Republican senators are privately discussing whether to delay a federal requirement that will force states to help fund the nation’s largest anti-hunger program, as your host scooped last week.

A proposal to postpone the implementation date of a GOP-led move to make states share the cost of SNAP benefits has emerged as a crucial factor that could garner the bipartisan support needed to move a farm bill through the Senate.

Democrats have insisted that the legislation delay the SNAP overhaul — which Republicans included in their domestic policy megabill last year — arguing it will kick people off the program and lead to benefit cuts.

They’ve also stressed the delay would put all states in the same boat, given that some states with lowest error rates won’t have to foot the bill at all and others with the highest error rates have an implementation delay built into the SNAP overhaul.

"I'm open to listening to their argument,” Boozman told MA last week. “It's just been very difficult to see where we'll be able to find the money to pay for that."

Including the cost-share delay is “the only way to get a farm bill through,” said one person close to the negotiations granted anonymity to discuss the private talks.

On the other side of the Capitol: Thompson, who has opposed attempts to delay the SNAP cost-share plan, said he trusts Boozman’s approach.

“He’s going to do whatever he needs to to get the 60 votes, and then we’ll go to conference committee,” Thompson told MA Thursday.

When asked if the House would support delaying the cost-share requirement, Thompson said he’d “reserve judgment.”

“I don’t think we should let states off the hook because the states are working hard,” he said. “And if they sense that we’re easing up, they may ease up, and that’s not good for the consumers.”

Some Republican senators and fiscal conservatives might not support the delay, given that they argued the cost-share requirement will force states to work harder to get their error rates down.

“If it makes economic sense to delay, it’s one thing,” Justice said. “But if all we’re doing is just putting it off for some political reason or whatever it may be, it’s not good with me.”
TRADE CORNER

USMCA IN FOCUS: U.S. and Mexican officials are set to have critical discussions about reauthorizing the United States-Canada-Mexico Agreement this week, after Mexican Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard confirmed meetings between the two sides would take place between May 27 and May 29, our Ari Hawkins writes in.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said last week that U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer would participate in meetings on May 27, according to reports, though a USTR official declined to comment on Greer’s schedule or confirm any meetings.

USTR also did not respond to a request for additional details about the talks, though Greer recently signaled the administration could push for stricter rules-of-origin requirements, which determine how much content must be produced in North America for a good to qualify for duty-free treatment under USMCA, Ari reports.

"If you're going to get a special ‌deal ⁠on trade with the United States of America, we want to make sure that there's U.S. content in that," he told reporters at a Micron Technology memory chip facility on Friday, according to a Reuters report.

This week’s talks come at a crucial time, just weeks before the first phase of the USMCA review begins on July 1.

The ag angle: The stakes of USMCA’s renewal are high for farm country, with Trump’s aggressive tariff rollout already creating market uncertainty for struggling producers, as farm lobbying groups have stressed.

Trump officials have promised ag priorities will remain top of mind during the review process — though lobbyists and industry groups are still watching closely.

“I think we'll do a tremendous job of making sure that U.S. farm interests are an important part of the overall review process,” Undersecretary of Agriculture for Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs Luke Lindberg told MA earlier this year.
Transitions

Austin Matheny-Kawesch is now press secretary for Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.). He was previously communications director for political affairs at the Environmental Defense Fund.

PESTICIDE POLITICS: Make America Healthy Again activists are claiming a victory after they successfully pushed to remove controversial protections for the pesticide industry from the House’s farm bill.

They’re keeping up the pressure as the legislation awaits a fierce Senate debate, even as Republican senators who support the pesticide industry’s requests acknowledge that including the protections would tank the package.

The House’s farm bill, led by Ag Chair G.T. Thompson (R-Pa.), originally contained a measure that would have barred states from enacting pesticide labeling laws stricter than federal standards. That language was a priority of the pesticide industry and agriculture group allies, who have described it as a crucial move to protect access to chemicals and maintain food affordability.

The House voted 280-142 in April on an amendment from Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) to remove the pesticide language from the farm bill amid a revolt from MAHA advocates, who contended it would shield chemical makers from thousands of lawsuits over their “failure to warn” of health risks.

It marked the MAHA movement’s first major win on pesticide policy on Capitol Hill — even in the face of President Donald Trump’s executive order promoting pesticide production earlier this year.

Luna said her Republican colleagues who voted against the amendment are “getting absolutely nuked” by MAHA moms.

“I think that they had a ‘come to Jesus’ moment,” Luna told MA in an interview in May. “And I'm happy that those moms are holding their feet to the fire, because how dare they.”

Despite the success in the House of removing the pesticide provision, Luna warned that some are still pushing for it. However, it would be a challenge to get to 60 Senate votes for a farm bill that includes the language, which some lawmakers have described as a poison pill.

“We are already hearing that in the Senate, some are saying that it shouldn't have been removed and trying to stick it back in,” she added. “And if that happens, there will be mutiny on the floor. The farm bill will get blown up. It will not pass.”

In the Senate: Sen. John Boozman (R-Ark.), who’s set to release his farm bill text this month, has told MA for months that he won’t be able to include the pesticide language and other contentious provisions in the Senate version.

“We need 60 votes to get a bill passed, and that’s really what we’re focusing on, is getting something passed,” Boozman said. “That makes [including] things like pesticides really difficult. These are things that I support. But again, there’s no bipartisan support for it.”

Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.), who sits on the Senate Ag Committee and chairs the Appropriations Ag-FDA subcommittee, also said he supports the language.

“And if we can include it, we’ll try,” Hoeven told MA in May. “I don’t know if we will be able to because of the Dems.”

But, but, but: Senators’ acknowledgment that the language would block farm bill passage hasn’t extinguished the hopes of some key supporters.

“There needs to be” a push to add the language back in, Thompson told MA recently.

“I hope that’s something that [the Senate] would consider addressing. It needs to be addressed,” he said. “The Luna amendment is a danger to the nation."

CropLife America, a pesticide maker trade group, said in a statement after the House’s farm bill vote that it would “strongly urge the Senate to restore and maintain these critical provisions.”

MAHA advocates are loudly opposing any efforts to add the pesticide language as negotiations progress.

“You will have to answer from hundreds and hundreds of moms in your community asking you why you were protecting foreign chemical companies over their children,” said Alex Clark, a prominent MAHA activist who hosts a podcast for Turning Point USA.

Why it matters: The MAHA movement’s success in the House and lobbying on the Senate farm bill illustrates its power, especially as long-standing alliances between Republicans and the agribusiness industry have backed the pesticide language.

Tony Lyons, president of MAHA Action, said during a recent call that the House vote was a “big triumph for the whole MAHA movement.”

Many vulnerable Republicans ended up voting for Luna’s amendment, including some from agriculture-heavy states — despite their colleagues’ arguments that the amendment would raise costs for farmers.

Those lawmakers faced a deluge of messages and calls from MAHA supporters ahead of the vote and decided not to risk backlash over language that was likely to be stripped from the final version of the bill, according to three people familiar with the behind-the-scenes discussions.

MA EXCLUSIVE: Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) will introduce six bills today to provide economic aid and bolster the federal safety net for specialty crop farmers.

“As California’s first senator to serve on the Senate Agriculture Committee in over 30 years, I'm fighting to address the needs of specialty crop farmers, which are very different than those of the commodity crops of the Midwest and the South,” Schiff said in a statement.

Schiff is pushing to include the bills in the Senate’s farm bill.

Specialty crop legislation is traditionally bipartisan, but the sector was deprioritized compared to row crops in the Trump administration’s farmer bridge program in 2025. USDA released the payment rates and enrollment period for the aid for specialty crop farmers on Friday. One of Schiff’s bills would provide an additional $5 billion for the producers.

Another bill in the package would establish a permanent specialty crop disaster program, replacing the practice of ad hoc congressional relief.

Other bills would boost pest management funding, set aside $30 million per year for sector technology research and aim to increase the competitiveness of U.S. specialty crops in foreign markets.

Top concerns: Democrats’ top objection to the bill has been spending cuts to fruit and vegetable benefits in a top food aid program, which they contend is at odds with the Trump administration’s MAHA agenda.

“I’m left asking, how on earth does ending that access to healthy food make America healthy again?” Rep. Sanford Bishop (D-Ga.), the Appropriations Ag-FDA subcommittee’s ranking member, said during the bill’s markup.

The cuts to the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children, which provides tailored nutrition to more than 6.5 million people, come after it was the only federal nutrition program to win praise in last year’s MAHA report.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told lawmakers at a House budget hearing in April that he was “not happy” with the planned cuts.

She said the federal government is conducting audits of Mexico's surveillance and movement controls and has dispatched mounted patrol officers and dogs to monitor animal crossings on the southern border.

A New World screwworm outbreak could hurt the GOP ahead of the midterms as it threatens to kill scores of cattle and raise the price of beef. Rollins tried to get out in front of the pest’s food supply implications after it was detected in the U.S. last week.

“This pest does not cause a food safety issue,” Rollins said on a press call Thursday. “The food supply is not compromised at all. This is not a disease, it is not a virus, it is simply an insect that lands in a wound and lays eggs that like to eat the flesh around the wound.”

Rollins tried to quell early fears about screwworm spiking the already high price of beef in a separate gaggle Thursday, saying technology and treatment methods have improved dramatically since the pest was largely eradicated from the U.S. in the 1960s.

“We're in a very different scenario that should allow us to spot, to confirm and then to treat without much if any disruption to the actual herd size and to beef prices,” Rollins said. 

Asked about a USDA economic impact report from January 2025 that estimated a screwworm outbreak could cost Texas producers over $732 million, Rollins said the economic impact for farmers will likely not be that severe.

“[The report] was assuming that we were going to be battling a full infestation and that we were going to have to completely stop all movement processing of any of our Texas cattle for a long period of time,” Rollins told reporters. “There is nothing right now that tells us that any of that will actually be the case in this instant. We are very confident today that we'll be able to one-off these.”

The containment timeline for the pest remains unclear as various state and federal entities work to collect data on the extent of the infestation, Michael Schmoyer, associate administrator for the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service and director of the New World Screwworm Directorate, said on a call with reporters.

Texas Animal Health Commission Executive Director Bud Dinges said his organization is conducting surveillance in the area of the detection to determine “how widespread the problem is” and “how long this infestation may last.”

GOP lawmakers pointed to past success at eradicating the pest and steps taken to prepare for an outbreak but are bracing themselves for a growing problem.

“I'm just afraid that the horse is out of the barn here, that wild animals are bringing the screwworm across,” Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) told MA.

The Natural Resources Conservation Service, the USDA agency that helps farmers with conservation projects on their land, lost 23 percent of its staff between January 2025 and January 2026, the report said. Over that period, 141 counties lost all of their NRCS staff.

ON THE BORDERLINE: Preemptive efforts to contain the New World screwworm outbreak have led to painful trade-offs — including the closure of the southern border to livestock imports for over a year.

The border will stay closed indefinitely, Ag Secretary Brooke Rollins said Thursday.

But the question of opening the border to livestock is quietly looming as screwworm dominates the industry’s attention, and some Republicans and state officials say reopening the border must not fall out of sight.

“We continue to have those discussions with USDA about properly reopening the border sooner rather than later,” New Mexico Agriculture Secretary Jeff Witte told MA.

“They understand the need and the impacts on commerce in both directions. There's some things that have to be settled in Mexico, and reassurances have to be made,” he added. “But everybody's on the same page that, in fact, the border does need to open.”

Some Republican lawmakers voiced similar stances: Reopening the U.S.-Mexico border to livestock imports remains high on their to-do list — with proper precautions.

“Probably what we could do to help bring down the cost of hamburger, though, is to open up our borders,” Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) said, adding that “the horse is out of the barn here” already with screwworm.

Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) said he supports opening parts of the border, specifically the western side, which is cooler and has “had zero screwworm problems.”

House Ag Chair G.T. Thompson (R-Pa.) said during a hearing with Rollins on June 4 that it is important to “have frank conversations about returning to a sense of normalcy at the border.” The closure has halted cattle imports from Mexico, leading it to build out its own meat processing infrastructure independent of the United States, Thompson said.

“We need to keep talking about next best steps for the southern border, including a reopening that includes rigorous checkpoints, treatment and quarantine measures,” Thompson said at the hearing.

Thompson later told MA that there are “probably at least a million head of cattle on the Mexican side that normally would be in the United States and in those feed lots in Texas.”

But, but, but: Rollins told reporters livestock restrictions on the southern border will remain firmly in place for the time being.

“We've had the ports closed for a year now, so we have not let any animals across the [southern] ports because it is so close to Texas, but we haven't let them in through New Mexico or Arizona either,” Rollins said. “That will obviously continue until we have a better understanding of what we're dealing with.”

Some Republicans said ramping livestock imports back up amid the parasite’s threat will only cause more pain.

Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) said easing restrictions on the border could increase the probability of further screwworm incursions, noting, “That consequence is deadly and will damage the supply of beef.” Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) expressed similar concern, saying Mexican cattle imports carry the threat of diminishing the U.S. herd.

USDA had confirmed 12 cases of screwworm in the U.S. as of Sunday night.

A spokesperson for the department told MA in a statement that “first and foremost, USDA is focused on containment and eventual eradication of NWS,” but the department is evaluating every day “the possibility of re-opening ports.”

Watch the interview.

 
 
NUTRITION PROGRAMS

MA Q&A: Federal food policy is reshaping the market for fruit and vegetable growers on multiple fronts. The Trump administration has reorganized the Food and Nutrition Administration, the USDA agency formerly called the Food and Nutrition Service that administers school meal programs, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children — programs that represent a major outlet for the produce industry.

A new school meal rule expected to be released later this summer could revise nutrition standards to align more closely with the new Dietary Guidelines for Americans.

Mollie Van Lieu, vice president of nutrition and health policy at the International Fresh Produce Association, spoke with MA about how her organization is navigating the changes.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What is IFPA’s stance on the recent reorganization of the Food and Nutrition Administration?

We're definitely watching that closely. Certainly the programs that FNS administers, particularly school meals and WIC, are really significant markets for the fruit and vegetable industry and American fruit and vegetable growers. So we're working with and speaking with child nutrition directors to make sure that they will continue to get the resources they need.

We definitely work with career staff, and we don't want to see research that's done on these programs reduced.

How is IPFA translating the Dietary Guidelines for Americans into its lobbying strategy on Capitol Hill?

The new dietary guidelines are pretty consistent with previous dietary guidelines as it relates to fruits and vegetables and serving amounts.

School meals definitely [are] impacted the most because you have to serve from all five vegetable subgroups. So that's something we're watching because in the new dietary guidelines, they didn't explicitly mention the five vegetable subgroups.

So with the administration announcing that they'll be putting out a new school meal rule, probably later this summer, we’ll see if that will impact the nutrition standards that require schools to serve vegetables from all five of those subgroups.

We're definitely talking to the Hill about that and what that has meant for us growers and just diversity of vegetables that kids are having access to.

What is IFPA’s stance on the new SNAP stocking standards rule?

Most traditional grocers, where 90 percent of people are redeeming SNAP benefits, easily meet the new stocking standards.

In the smaller [stores] where there are barriers, we also have to make sure that we're spurring demand, too, because people can't eat something that they don't have access to. We're willing to work with those retailers that might be having challenges.

OPEN RANGE: USDA directed U.S. Forest Service employees to expand grazing access on National Forest System lands, advising field offices to reopen vacant and closed allotments and streamline permitting to increase grazing capacity.

The order advances a March memorandum of understanding between Rollins and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to boost the domestic cattle herd.

Rollins framed the move as a rebuke of regulatory creep.

“For too long, bureaucratic overreach and activist-driven lawfare have undermined the multiple-use mandate of our National Forests and Grasslands,” Rollins in a statement on the directive.

The directive also called for better coordination with permittees during wildfires and more flexibility on drought relief grazing.

Presented by U.S. Farmers & Ranchers in Action: Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Rachel Shin

Presented by U.S. Farmers & Ranchers in Action

With help from Grace Yarrow and Marcia Brown

President Donald Trump told reporters on June 10 that he may terminate USMCA because “we don't need anything that Canada has, we don’t need anything that Mexico has.” | Getty Images
QUICK FIX

— Ag Republicans are urging the White House to renew the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, in light of President Donald Trump’s indication that he would not.

— The Senate farm bill text is poised to drop tomorrow.

— Maine had a plan to feed its hungry. Then came Trump's “big beautiful bill.”

IT’S MONDAY, JUNE 22. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Rachel Shin. Send tips and pitches to rshin@politico.com, get in touch securely on Signal at rshin.80 and follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.
 

A message from U.S. Farmers & Ranchers in Action:

A new S&P Global Energy analysis, commissioned by U.S. Farmers and Ranchers in Action, explores how expanded biofuel markets could help create new demand for agriculture, strengthen energy and food security, and power long-term growth. Discover what the future could look like by 2050. Read the report.
 

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

TRADE TROUBLES: Farm-state Republicans are urging Trump to reconsider his stance on USMCA after he suggested he would abandon the trade deal weeks ahead of its July mandatory review.

Senate Ag Chair John Boozman (R-Ark.) told your host that he has spoken with the White House and is “encouraging that we get a new commitment signed as soon as possible.”

“USMCA is very important, and I think that the president will ultimately negotiate a good deal,” Boozman said. “It was one of his centerpiece achievements of his last administration.”

Trump told reporters on June 10 that he was erring on the side of terminating the trade agreement because “we don't need anything that Canada has, we don’t need anything that Mexico has.”

The Trump administration is conducting formal negotiations with Mexico and recently opened discussions with Canada as part of the six-year review of USMCA. Under the deal’s “sunset review” provision, all three countries must meet on July 1 to say whether they want to renew the pact for another 16 years.

Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) told MA that she hopes “the White House is going to reconsider” letting the deal expire because USMCA is “a wonderful trade agreement for our ag producers.” Other senators similarly emphasized the deal has been a boon to American farmers and the broader economies of the participating nations.

“It's pretty clear to me, and I hope everybody else, even the president of the United States, that … it's beneficial to all three countries,” Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) told reporters last week.

Republicans are holding out hope that despite Trump’s suggestions that he will not renew USMCA, he will change his mind come July. Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.) said his negative comments about the pact may have just been “Art of the Deal”-style gamesmanship.

“The president likes to keep the other party off balance in any negotiation,” Hoeven said. “I think that may be his negotiating style so that they don’t assume we’re going to get it just the way it is.”

Key context: If one or more countries object to renewing USMCA, the agreement would expire in 2036, unless negotiators resolve outstanding concerns in annual reviews over the next 10 years.

Any of the countries could terminate the agreement with six months’ notice, though both Mexico and Canada have sent letters to the Trump administration saying they support renewing the deal.
 

A message from U.S. Farmers & Ranchers in Action:
 
On the Hill

FARM BILL INCOMING: Boozman is set to release his farm bill text tomorrow, according to three people familiar with the conversations, Grace reports. The bill will tee up a fight over Democrats’ nutrition demands and some Republican priorities that aren’t expected to be included.

Committee staff will privately brief Senate Agriculture Committee members and industry groups today ahead of the bill's introduction, according to the people, who were granted anonymity to discuss the private plans.

Boozman’s plan is expected to omit some controversial GOP priorities in an effort to secure enough Democratic support to clear the Senate’s 60-vote threshold.

Boozman said he is aiming to mark up the bill between the chamber's Fourth of July and August recesses.

The sticking point: Democrats have said they will not support a farm bill package that doesn’t delay the implementation of a provision included in the GOP’s domestic policy package that will soon force some states to foot part of the bill for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits. It’s not clear whether Boozman’s base text will include the SNAP cost-share delay.

“I don't know that the chairman has made a decision on if it has to be a partisan markup,” said one ag lobbyist familiar with the talks, also granted anonymity to discuss them.

Republicans’ megalaw already granted a group of states with the highest SNAP error rates an implementation delay to give them more time to reduce inaccurate payments. States with error rates under 6 percent won’t have to foot the bill at all.

“The real challenge is the fact that Republicans have already made an exception,” the lobbyist noted. “If there was no exception, I think they would have an easier time holding the line, but the political dynamics are just tough.”
 

J.B. Pritzker talks Democrats’ road ahead

On On the Road, Jonathan Martin sits down with Gov. J.B. Pritzker at Manny’s Deli for a candid conversation on 2028 speculation, party strategy and the future of Democratic politics.
Watch now.

 
 
SNAP CHATS

THE FOOD SECURITY OUTLOOK: Last year’s passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act has set in motion one of the biggest transformations of the welfare state that the U.S. has seen in decades.

For more than a generation, SNAP — which provides roughly 40 million people with money for groceries — has served as the country’s dominant vector for direct payments to people struggling to eat. But SNAP’s era as arguably the nation’s preeminent anti-poverty program may be ending.

Already 3.5 million people nationwide have been booted from the program, and as the law’s new eligibility terms take effect this year, more are likely to follow, while others will be abruptly sent back into a workforce for which they are unprepared. Roughly 45,000 people in Maine, including veterans and homeless adults — briefly granted a reprieve from work requirements during the Biden administration — will be newly required to work or volunteer.

In few places has the response been as swift as in Maine, where Democratic Gov. Janet Mills, legislative leaders and state nonprofits seven years ago committed to a 2030 goal of ensuring Mainers always have enough to eat. Now that ambitious objective — one that officials and activists believed was within reach for a small state with a motivated government, even after pandemic-era setbacks — seems even further away.

Instead, lawmakers, nonprofits and bureaucrats now see themselves spending the remainder of the decade trying to manage the impact of a federal law that will make it harder for millions of people to obtain federal nutrition assistance and health care while passing significant costs onto states.

“What makes it difficult is knowing it’s not sustainable,” said Maine Speaker of the House Ryan Fecteau at the state house, bleary-eyed in a worn long-sleeve tee and vest after presiding over several days of late-night sessions in April to deliver the budget and other priorities.

Read Marcia’s full magazine piece here.

item.content:encoded:
Delivered every Monday by 10 a.m., Weekly Agriculture examines the latest news in agriculture and food politics and policy.
 

By Marcia Brown

With help from Ellie Borst
QUICK FIX

— The Supreme Court ruling allowing the Trump administration to end temporary protected status for more than 1 million immigrants could make it harder for meatpackers and others in the food supply chain to hire enough workers.

— The Make America Healthy Again movement isn’t satisfied by President Donald Trump’s executive order promoting regenerative agriculture.

— Confirmed New World screwworm cases in the United States are ticking up.  

IT’S MONDAY, JUNE 29. Welcome to Morning Agriculture! I’m your host, Marcia Brown. Send tips to marciabrown@politico.com and get in touch securely on Signal at marciagbrown.68. Don’t forget to follow us at @Morning_Ag for more.

Want to receive this newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro. You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.
DRIVING THE DAY

TEMPORARY PROTECTED STATUS: A Supreme Court ruling last week that will make it easier for the Trump administration to deport certain immigrants could also add new labor market pressures in the food supply chains, analysts say.

The decision could pave the way for Trump to end temporary protected status for people from Syria and Haiti and also make it easier for Trump to end TPS for people from countries facing war, natural disasters or other challenges. The ruling could upend the lives of roughly a million people and may make it harder for meatpackers and other employers to find enough people to work.

Nearly a third of meatpacking workers in the U.S. are foreign-born, according to the Migration Policy Institute, and many of those hold temporary protected status, an immigration designation that allows people to live and work legally in the U.S.

“The effects of this ruling will be felt by more than just those directly impacted — every worker, every community and the entire economy will feel it,” said Milton Jones, president of the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union. “It jeopardizes worker and food safety in meatpacking plants, food processing facilities and grocery stores, with workers left behind being pushed to their limit without the skilled hands of their immigrant co-workers next to them.”

With the court’s blessing, the Trump administration can begin deportation proceedings against Syrians and Haitians, if they cannot obtain another legal status, such as asylum or work visas. Other TPS recipients from countries like Venezuela and Afghanistan are also expected to be affected by the court’s ruling. Many have lived in the U.S. for decades and have children who are U.S. citizens.

Terminating TPS, combined with ending other refugee and humanitarian programs, could result in a 20 percent cut in jobs at poultry plants in the Delmarva Peninsula, according to a warning from Mountaire Farms’ executive Zach Evans obtained by Civil Eats this year.

“The Supreme Court ruling is likely to further stress the labor supply at meatpacking plants across the country,” Alejandro Gutierrez-Li, an immigration economist at North Carolina State University, told MA, noting that meatpackers can’t easily access the H-2A visa program for year-round work like meatpacking. “Research has shown that, even in periods of high unemployment, Americans prefer to pass on physically demanding jobs at meatpacking plants.”

“If you look at the history of the industry, it’s basically been built on immigrant labor for a century, going back to the late 1800s,” said Derrell Peel, an agricultural economist at Oklahoma State University focused on the beef industry.

The meatpacking industry downplayed the impact of the TPS ruling. 

“Our members have largely transitioned away from this workforce,” said Sarah Little, a spokesperson for the Meat Institute, a trade group that represents large meatpacking companies. “The ruling will not have much impact on the industry as a whole at this stage.”

Still, the Supreme Court ruling comes at a time when beef meatpackers are paying record prices for cattle and losing money. Meatpackers have already raised wages and benefits since the coronavirus pandemic as they aim to recruit more workers to jobs that are difficult and dangerous.

What’s next: It's not clear how quickly the administration will act, but UFCW is urging the administration to give TPS recipients more time to plan “before forcing them to leave their homes.”

Gutierrez-Li noted the labor market pressures could eventually be passed on to consumers in the form of higher consumer prices and lead the U.S. to increase beef imports.

“Plants that are not capable of replacing their TPS workers may decide to close,” he told MA. “In rural areas with few employers, this could have broader negative impacts on the local economy.”

Michelle Mittelstadt, a spokesperson for the Migration Policy Institute, said “only Congress” can act to create more permanent immigration protections for Haitian and Syrian TPS recipients, but it would need three-fifths of the Senate as required by the Immigration Act of 1990, “which seems quite unlikely in the current political environment.”
At the White House

Trump signed an order late Thursday aimed at reducing farm chemical use on food crops, a gesture toward a disillusioned MAHA coalition, Ellie Borst of POLITICO’s E&E News reports.

The executive order establishes advancing "private-sector innovation in farm modernization" and other regenerative agriculture practices as U.S. policy. But it stops short of many regulatory changes pushed by MAHA advocates, who are challenging Trump's allegiance to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s mission to reduce risky chemical exposures.

"This EO does nothing for chemical regulation but kick the can down the road," said Vani Hari, a MAHA influencer and food blogger with a close relationship to Kennedy, in a post on X.

The executive order came the same day the Supreme Court sided with Bayer, which makes Roundup, in a decision that makes it harder for people to sue the company. Bayer has been facing billions of dollars in liability from lawsuits alleging Roundup, the brand name for glyphosate, causes cancer.

The White House had sided with industry in an amicus brief, as Pamela King and your host reported, sparking MAHA’s ire. But the court’s decision made a preplanned dinner last week at the White House for regenerative farmers a bit … awkward.

Guests’ party favors? Organic seed packets.

The Trump administration has sought to balance the priorities of a longtime GOP constituency, farmers, while pleasing the president’s relatively new allies in the MAHA movement. The same day of the executive order, USDA also announced a new regulation that would allow regenerative farmers to access premium prices in biofuels markets.

Trade groups celebrated the new rule.

“This new rule is an important step forward, and we believe it will help jumpstart opportunities for growers who are committed to doing what’s right for the land and the environment, while being recognized for their efforts,” Mark Mueller, an Iowa farmer and president of the Iowa Corn Growers Association, said in a statement.

SPEAKING OF MAHA: Our Jessie Blaeser has an illuminating new analysis of what The POLITICO Poll revealed about the MAHA movement. Even MAHA supporters are divided over reducing vaccines, she noted, and while many MAHA principles have support across the political spectrum, the issue of reducing vaccines shows the biggest partisan split.

On the other hand, there’s broad support for a lot of MAHA principles, including eating more healthy food and reducing exposure to harmful chemicals, even among people who don’t identify as part of MAHA.
AROUND THE AGENCIES

THE NEXT TURN OF THE SCREW(WORM): At least 27 cases of the New World screwworm have been detected in New Mexico and Texas, with new cases popping up over the last week, according to the latest numbers from USDA.

The larvae have been found in cattle, sheep, goats and one dog. The pest can be deadly for livestock, and monitoring, treatment and prevention are costly for ranchers.

While the New World screwworm was regularly found in the U.S. in the 1960s, the production of sterile male flies, which drive down the population by mating with female flies, previously eradicated the pest from the U.S.

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins joined Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Saturday for the opening of a new facility in Chiapas, Mexico, designed to contain the spread of the flesh-eating pest. The facility will produce 100 million sterile flies weekly by the fall, but former USDA officials have said the Trump administration’s internal federal spending reviews delayed its opening — and that it could have been open as early as this spring, as your host previously reported.

The new facility will double the current capacity for sterile fly production, but experts have said it’s still not enough to push the fly out of the U.S.

USDA demurred when asked about a timeline for U.S. eradication. Dudley Hoskins, the department’s undersecretary for marketing and regulatory programs, recently told the Texas House Agriculture and Livestock Committee that 500 million sterile flies are needed to drive out the pest.

A third USDA facility in Texas intended to produce more sterile flies is not yet online.

According to USDA, Rollins may hold another screwworm press briefing, “likely this week.”

FIRST IN MA: Anti-monopoly and progressive groups including the American Economic Liberties Project and Demand Progress are sending a letter to Senate Ag Committee leaders today urging them to oppose including any version of the Save Our Bacon Act, language that would preempt state animal welfare laws like California’s Proposition 12, in the farm bill. The Senate farm bill does not include the language, but the House version does.
Row Crops

— Reps. G.T. Thompson (R-Pa.) and Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Mich.) introduced the Local Foods for Healthy Schools Act, which would reinstate a program that the Trump administration canceled last year.

— The DOJ sued four states led by Democratic governors, demanding they turn over the sensitive data of food aid applicants to USDA, your host reported.

— USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service issued a public health alert for ready-to-eat chicken Caesar wrap products for potential listeria contamination. USDA didn’t request a recall because the products are no longer for sale.

— Rollins sent a letter to New York Gov. Kathy Hochul asking about the “rapid expansion of large-scale solar development on New York farmland.”
